findings.summary: RESOLVED (attempt 1 item). The SEC-3 consequence no longer claims envelope-metadata tampering is detected and now matches the source of record and the code.
findings.detail: The overclaim sentence ('metadata tampering is detected by the version/authority handling, not by the hash') is gone. The reworded '- Consequence:' bullet (docs/limitations.md:406-413) now states: the hash detects only PayloadJson corruption; the envelope reader separately validates only SchemaVersion; Kind, RecordId, and Authority are not validated by the envelope; Terminal/UpdatedUtc are trusted by retention (StateRetention.IsTerminalAndExpired); metadata tampering is therefore not detected by the hash, which bounds StateEnvelopeCodec to a corruption detector rather than a tamper MAC; not an escalation because local write access to the state root is already the administrative boundary; optional post-V1 hardening to cover the metadata in the hash. Independent code verification: StateEnvelopeCodec.TryDeserialize compares the SHA-256 against parsed.PayloadJson only (StateEnvelopeCodec.cs:88); TryReadEnvelope rejects only a mismatched SchemaVersion (lines 144-149); StateRepository.Read discards the parsed envelope (out _) and derives paths from caller arguments, so Kind/RecordId/Authority are never validated (StateRepository.cs:58-83); StateRetention.IsTerminalAndExpired reads envelope.Terminal and envelope.UpdatedUtc (StateRetention.cs:164). The wording also matches security-review.json finding SEC-3 ('Retention trusts the unauthenticated Terminal and UpdatedUtc fields', 'corruption detection rather than tamper authentication') and release-review.attempt-3.json RR-20/RR-22. grep for 'is detected'/'tamper' shows only the corrected, negated statements. No overclaim remains.
